title: Adaptive column affordances and skeleton states for deep tables
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Our existing table components display abrupt blank areas when rows or columns are streamed in by the virtualized renderer. Users on slow connections or with large datasets experience jarring layout jumps and misplaced affordances (resize handles, sort chevrons).

Goal: Introduce an adaptive approach that combines per-column affordance modes (full, compact, minimal) with a robust skeleton/loading state that (a) reserves visual space for yet-to-render columns and rows, (b) surfaces contextual header controls only when relevant, and (c) maintains keyboard and screen-reader discoverability. This should reduce perceived jitter, improve discoverability of column actions, and keep density tokens consistent across modes.

Scope: Design tokens (spacing, motion durations, opacity tokens), header micro-interactions (hover/keyboard focus, touch hit targets), skeleton variants for row and header cells, and a lightweight affordance state machine consumed by the runtime to avoid costly reflows. Deliverables include Figma components, updated component docs, accessibility guidance, and handoff guidelines for engineering on instrumentation hooks and measurable success metrics.
success_criteria: Reduce perceived layout shift in large datasets by >40% (measured by internal demo traces)
Header action discovery rate +10% in usability test (n=12)
No regressions in keyboard navigation and screen reader flow (a11y audit pass)
Design tokens updated and merged with DS token spec
decisions: Use three affordance modes: full (desktop edit-heavy), compact (default for medium density), minimal (mobile/very dense) to limit DOM controls rendered by virtualization window
Skeletons reserve column width using --table-col-reserve token (derived from layout and minWidth rather than content) to prevent reflow when column becomes visible
Header controls should be lazy-rendered: presentational chevron exists always for layout but interactive elements are upgraded on hover/focus or when column enters viewport
Motion reduced for reduced-motion users: skeleton crossfade instead of translate/scale animations
tradeoffs: Lazy-rendering interactive controls reduces initial JS cost but adds micro-latency on first interaction. We accept a small (~50ms) first-interaction bump for better overall throughput under high concurrency.
Skeletons reserve width conservatively; for very dynamic column resizing this can introduce slight over-padding. Engineering should provide heuristics to tighten reserve after first paint.
Three-mode affordance system adds complexity to Design System docs and component props but keeps runtime choices explicit and predictable for infra teams.
accessibility_notes: All affordance modes must expose header actions via keyboard (Enter/Space to open menu) and a single consistent focus order for screen readers
Skeletons must include aria-busy on the table container and aria-live polite region for row insertion events to announce new content without noise
Touch targets remain >= 44px in compact mode; minimal mode collapses to 32px with long-press fallback for secondary actions
engineering_handoff: Suggested API flags: affordanceMode: 'full'|'compact'|'minimal', skeletonMode: 'reserve'|'overlay', headerUpgradeTrigger: 'hover'|'focus'|'viewport'

Engineering notes: provide a small 'layout-reserve' CSS custom property per column, expose first-paint hook to update reserve widths, and instrument first-interaction latency metric (metric name: table.header.first_interaction_ms)
